metaDescription: Six cordless circular saws at or under $200 from DEWALT, Makita, RYOBI and DEKOPRO compared on blade size, brushless motors, depth of cut and platform.
expertTake: The DEWALT DCS590B is the pick for most buyers because a brushless motor, 2-9/16 inch depth of cut and a mature 20V MAX platform make it a real framing saw without a cord. The RYOBI ONE+ HP is the value pick if you already own 18V ONE+ batteries, since it matches the DEWALT's depth at a lower platform cost. Skip this bracket if you rip 2x lumber all day, because even the best battery saw drains packs fast under that load and a corded or 60V saw is the better tool. The extra budget over a basic saw mostly buys brushless efficiency and a deeper battery platform.
introParagraphs: A cordless circular saw replaces the cord with a battery, and for a lot of work that trade is excellent: no extension cord, no tripping, no outlet hunt on a roof. The catch is that a saw is one of the hungriest tools a battery can power, so the pack and the motor matter far more than the headline blade size.

This guide explains what a modest budget buys in a cordless circular saw, why blade diameter, depth of cut and motor type decide what the saw can really cut, and where bare-tool listings mislead. The picks are listed above, with the reviews below. Listing prices move, and the cap reflects prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: DEWALT DCS590B 20V MAX XR Brushless 7-1/4 Inch Circular Saw (Tool Only)
products.description:
A 7-1/4 inch blade with 2-9/16 inches of depth at 90 degrees is the standard full-size circular saw capacity, and it cuts through a 2x4 in one pass and a doubled 2x in two. The brushless motor spins at 5,500 RPM with no load, and the listing quotes up to 1,700 MWO, DEWALT's measure of power at the blade. That is a corded-class figure, and it explains why this saw lasts longer per charge than a brushed model.

The tradeoff is the bare tool listing. You get the saw and nothing else, so you need 20V MAX batteries, and a 5.0 Ah pack or larger is the right match for sustained framing cuts. Versus the older DCS391B, the XR model is the stronger and more efficient saw. Versus the RYOBI ONE+ HP, the DEWALT adds a more established platform at a higher price.

Ownership: the platform is the long-term value. Keep the blade sharp, because a dull blade drains a pack twice as fast as a sharp one. Clean sawdust from the shoe and guard pivot, check that the lower guard snaps back quickly, and store packs half charged. Many framers keep two packs on rotation, one in the saw and one on the charger, which turns a bare tool into a full-day setup.
products.bestFor: Framers and serious DIYers who already own 20V MAX batteries.
pros: Brushless motor reaches 5,500 RPM and extends runtime
2-9/16 inch depth cuts a 2x4 in one pass
Mature 20V MAX platform has tools for every job
Quoted 1,700 MWO suits framing loads
cons: Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Heavier with a large battery than 6-1/2 inch saws
Highest relative price among the 20V MAX picks

products.name: RYOBI ONE+ HP 18V Brushless 7-1/4 Inch Circular Saw (Tool Only)
products.description:
A brushless motor at 5,000 RPM drives a 7-1/4 inch blade through 2-9/16 inches of wood at 90 degrees, matching the DEWALT's capacity and giving up only a few hundred RPM. The listing claims up to 370 cuts per charge, a figure that depends on the pack and the wood. Bevel detents at six angles, including 15, 22-1/2, 30, 45 and 56 degrees, make angle work quick and repeatable.

The key tradeoff is the platform and the bare listing. ONE+ batteries are widely available and economical, but you must own them or buy them. Next to the DEWALT DCS590B, the RYOBI is a smaller step down in raw speed and a bigger step down in price, which is why it is the value choice for homeowners. A 45 degree depth of 1-13/16 inches is competitive.

Ownership: if you already own ONE+ batteries, this saw is almost a bonus. Keep the blade clean of pitch, and use a good blade instead of the stock one. Check the bevel lock and the detent mechanism for debris, and avoid bouncing the saw on its side, since the guard can crack. A good habit is to mark the bevel detent you use most with tape, since the detent levers on any saw can be hard to read in sunlight.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who already own RYOBI ONE+ batteries and want a full-size brushless saw.
pros: Brushless 7-1/4 inch saw matches the DEWALT's depth of cut
Six bevel detents speed up angle cuts
ONE+ batteries are widely available and economical
Quoted 370 cuts per charge suits remodeling jobs
cons: Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Slightly lower RPM than the DEWALT
Platform is geared to homeowners rather than daily trades

products.name: DEWALT FLEXVOLT 60V MAX DCS578B 7-1/4 Inch Circular Saw with Brake

specList.label: Power claim
specList.value: Up to 47% more than the DCS575

products.description:
FLEXVOLT batteries switch between 20V and 60V depending on the tool, and this saw runs at 60V for corded-class power. The listing claims 47 percent more power than the DCS575, and the electric brake stops the blade quickly after you release the trigger. A 57 degree bevel capacity is the widest in this roundup, which helps with roof framing and angle work.

The tradeoff is cost and weight. FLEXVOLT batteries are large and expensive, and a bare tool listing means you must already own them. Compared with the DCS590B, the FLEXVOLT is stronger but also heavier. If you own FLEXVOLT packs for other tools, this saw is the strongest cordless circular saw you can buy near this price.

Ownership: a brake needs a clean mechanism, so blow out sawdust regularly. FLEXVOLT batteries should be stored away from heat, and you can use them in 20V tools too. Keep a spare blade handy, and swap them when cuts burn. Because FLEXVOLT packs are expensive, check whether you would use them on other tools before choosing this saw over the DCS590B.
products.bestFor: Framers who already own FLEXVOLT packs and want the strongest cordless saw.
pros: 60V power approaches the output of a corded saw
Electric brake stops the blade quickly
57 degree bevel is the widest in the roundup
FLEXVOLT packs also run 20V tools
cons: Bare tool, and FLEXVOLT packs are large and costly

products.name: Makita XSH03Z 18V LXT Brushless 6-1/2 Inch Circular Saw (Tool Only)
products.description:
A 6-1/2 inch blade is smaller than the 7-1/4 inch standard, which makes the saw lighter and quieter and reduces cutting depth to about 2-1/8 inches. Automatic Speed Change senses load and adjusts speed and torque during the cut, so the saw slows in dense wood and speeds up in light cuts. The brushless motor runs cooler and wastes less battery.

The trade is capacity. A 6-1/2 inch saw cannot cut through a doubled 2x in one pass, which the DEWALT can in two. Makita's 18V LXT platform is deep and well regarded, and it is a smart base for a long-term collection. If your work is trim, plywood and decking, a lighter saw is a better fit than a framing saw.

Ownership: the saw is built to run on LXT batteries, which cover a vast tool range. Check the blade guard and blade fit, since a 6-1/2 inch blade is a different size from 7-1/4. Keep a thin-kerf blade on it for the best runtime. The automatic speed feature is most noticeable in knotty lumber, where the saw eases off instead of bogging and then recovers.
products.bestFor: Remodelers and trim carpenters who value light weight and a deep 18V platform.
pros: Automatic Speed Change adjusts to the load during the cut
6-1/2 inch blade makes the saw lighter and more nimble
Brushless motor runs cool and saves battery
LXT platform is deep and well supported
cons: Shallower cut depth than 7-1/4 inch saws
Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Higher relative price for a smaller saw

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX DCS391B 6-1/2 Inch Circular Saw (Tool Only)
products.description:
A magnesium shoe is a base plate that stays flat and resists bending, which keeps cuts square after years of jobsite abuse. The 5,150 RPM motor is a brushed design, so it spins as fast as the brushless saws but wastes more battery. The listing highlights a rubber overmolded grip for balance, and the 6-1/2 inch blade keeps the weight down.

Compared with the DCS590B, this is the older and simpler saw. It does not offer the longer runtime of brushless, but it costs less and shares 20V MAX batteries. Versus the Makita XSH03Z, it lacks automatic speed change. For DIY projects such as shelves and a deck, it is a sensible way into the platform.

Ownership: because it is a bare tool, check battery compatibility, since the saw does not come with a pack. Brushes eventually wear, so plan on service after heavy use. Keep the shoe clean and check blade alignment occasionally. Remember that a bare tool is not a kit, so confirm your battery fits the saw before ordering.
products.bestFor: DIYers who own 20V MAX packs and want an inexpensive, solid saw.
pros: Magnesium shoe stays flat and keeps cuts square
5,150 RPM motor cuts quickly in plywood and lumber
Shares batteries with the 20V MAX platform
Light 6-1/2 inch body suits long overhead cuts
cons: Brushed motor drains batteries faster than brushless
Shallower depth than a 7-1/4 inch saw
Tool only, so batteries cost extra

buyingCriteria.criterion: Blade size and depth of cut
buyingCriteria.explanation: A 7-1/4 inch blade cuts 2-9/16 inches deep at 90 degrees, enough for a 2x4 in one pass. A 6-1/2 inch blade, as on the Makita XSH03Z and DEWALT DCS391B, cuts about 2-1/8 inches and weighs less. At a 45 degree bevel depth drops by about a third, as the RYOBI's 1-13/16 inches shows. Choose 7-1/4 inch for framing and 6-1/2 inch for plywood and trim. A quick field check: set the depth so the blade extends about a quarter inch below the board, which keeps the exposed blade short and the cut cleaner.

Brushless motors waste less energy as heat, so a given battery makes more cuts. The DEWALT DCS590B, RYOBI HP and Makita XSH03Z are brushless, while the DCS391B is not. A saw works the motor harder than most tools, so the efficiency gain is larger here than in a drill. If you cut daily, brushless is worth the premium. Heat is the quiet cost of a brushed motor in a saw, because wasted energy turns into warmth in the housing and into shorter pack life.

A 2.0 Ah pack cuts a handful of boards, while 5.0 Ah and larger packs run a framing session. Most listings here are bare tools, so budget for packs. Platform breadth matters, and the DEWALT, RYOBI and Makita families are all wide. A pack that has sat unused for a season may need a full charge cycle before it delivers its rated runtime, so charge before the first big job.

Bevel capacity is how far the shoe tilts, and detents make common angles repeatable. The RYOBI has six detents and the FLEXVOLT reaches 57 degrees. A saw without positive stops at 22.5 and 45 degrees wastes time on angle cuts. Setting a bevel by the scale alone is rarely accurate, so check with a speed square before cutting good lumber.

An electric brake stops the blade within a second of releasing the trigger, which reduces risk and saves time. The FLEXVOLT DCS578B has one. A lower guard that snaps back freely is a basic safety feature, and sawdust can gum it up. Even with a brake, wait for the blade to stop before setting the saw down.

The saw's listed weight excludes the battery, and a large pack adds a pound or more. Light saws like the 6-1/2 inch models reduce fatigue during long overhead cuts. Check the weight with the battery you will actually use. Add the weight of the pack to the listing weight when comparing saws, because a large pack can add nearly a quarter of the total.

specDecoder.meaning: MWO is DEWALT's measure of power delivered to the blade. It is a peak figure, not a sustained one.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DCS590B's 1,700 MWO is not comparable to a RYOBI or Makita RPM claim.

specDecoder.meaning: RPM is blade speed with nothing cutting. It drops under load, and a brushless motor holds speed better.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DCS590B's 5,500 RPM is a no-load number.

specDecoder.meaning: This is a manufacturer's estimate of cuts on a specific battery in a specific material. Results vary with the wood and blade.
specDecoder.watchFor: The RYOBI's 370 and DEWALT's 368 are best-case numbers.

specDecoder.spec: Depth of cut at 90 and 45 degrees
specDecoder.meaning: Depth is how thick a board the blade can pass through at a given bevel. It falls as the shoe tilts.
specDecoder.watchFor: A listing that quotes only 90 degree depth hides the shallower 45 degree number.

specDecoder.meaning: Tool only means the saw ships without a battery or charger. It makes sense if you already own the platform.
specDecoder.watchFor: Five of the six picks here are tool only.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared blade size and depth of cut, from the 7-1/4 inch saws at 2-9/16 inches to the 6-1/2 inch saws at about 2-1/8 inches. Capacity decides which jobs the saw can finish.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated brushless from brushed motors, since runtime is the main limit of cordless saws. The DCS391B is the only brushed saw.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform value
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed battery family breadth, from DEWALT 20V MAX and FLEXVOLT to RYOBI ONE+ and Makita LXT.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at brakes, bevel detents and guard design, which affect accuracy and safety.

howWeEvaluated.title: Relative value
howWeEvaluated.description: We used price tier to compare what extra spending buys. Higher tiers bring brushless motors and larger capacity.

cards.label: 7-1/4 inch
cards.text: Cuts 2-9/16 inches deep and handles framing lumber. The DCS590B, RYOBI HP and FLEXVOLT DCS578B fall here.

cards.label: 6-1/2 inch
cards.text: Lighter and quieter, but about 2-1/8 inches deep. The Makita XSH03Z and DEWALT DCS391B fall here.

howToChoose.note: Choose 7-1/4 inch for framing and 6-1/2 inch for plywood, trim and overhead work.

howToChoose.subheading: For Cutting Decking and Framing Lumber Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Framing needs full depth, a brushless motor and large batteries. Wet pressure-treated lumber is the worst case for runtime.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DCS590B and RYOBI HP cut a 2x in one pass, and the FLEXVOLT is the strongest. The 6-1/2 inch saws need two passes on doubled lumber.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cut framing daily. The DCS590B and FLEXVOLT DCS578B show what pro-grade runtime looks like.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cut plywood occasionally. The DEWALT DCS391B or RYOBI HP covers that.

maintenance.task: Replace the blade when cuts burn
maintenance.why: A dull blade drains batteries and burns wood. Thin-kerf blades extend runtime.
Sawdust jams the lower guard. A sticky guard is a safety risk.
A bent shoe gives angled cuts. Replace it if it wobbles.
Heat and full charge age cells. Cool storage keeps capacity.
Dust blocks cooling and hurts runtime. Compressed air clears it.

faq.q: Can a cordless saw replace a corded saw?
faq.a: For most jobs, yes. Brushless saws on large batteries match corded saws for short sessions. For all-day ripping, corded still wins. Many professionals now run cordless saws for most framing, keeping a corded saw for long ripping days.
It buys brushless 7-1/4 inch saws as bare tools, or smaller saws in kits. Listing prices move, so check the live cost.

faq.q: How long do these saws last?
faq.a: Brushless saws last longer. Batteries wear first. Keep packs cool. Avoid leaving packs in a hot truck, since heat is the biggest enemy of lithium cells.
For trim and plywood, yes. For framing, 7-1/4 inch is better.
It is a safety and time-saving feature. The FLEXVOLT has one.
A thin-kerf framing blade gives the best runtime. Finish blades suit plywood. Carbide-tipped blades with 24 teeth rip faster and 40 to 60 teeth give smoother crosscuts.
